---
title: "Is Average Adjusted Gross Income per Tax Return Associated with the Percentage EV Registration Across California Zip codes in 2023?"
# subtitle: "Subtitle"
author: "Hien Vo"
thanks: "Project repository available at: https://github.com/HVoH/Math261A-Project1"
date: today
date-format: long
abstract: "California is one of the largest markets for electric vehicles (EVs) in the US. However, EV adoption varies across different areas of the state. Because EVs are generally more expensive to purchase than many other types of vehicles, income may be associated with EV adoption. This study uses linear regression to investigate whether EV registration is associated with average adjusted gross income (AGI). Using 2023 income data and individual EV registration data aggregated by Zip code, the analysis examine whether the areas with higher average AGI tend to have a higher percentage of EV registrations. The fitted model estimates an increase of approximately 0.1378 percentage points in EV registration share for each $10,000 increase in average AGI, with an R-squared value of 0.3446. Although the association is statistically significant, residual diagnostics indicate violations of model assumptions, limiting the reliability of the simple linear regression model." 

format: pdf

# Introduction

Following the adoption of California's zero-emission vehicles policies, the required percentage of new zero-emission vehicle sales is scheduled to increase gradually, reaching 100% by 2035. Although the government has programs such that the Enhanced Fleet Modernization Program ("EFMP") that provides subsidies to EV buyers, the price of EVs may still be an important factors in purchasing decisions. Muehlegger and Rapson (2022) finds that EV demand from low- and middle-income buyers is price-elastic. Their research shows that if subsidies resulted in a reductions of 10% in EV prices, sales to low- and middle income buyers would increase by approximately 21%. They also emphasize EVs price impacts on this customer segments more than higher-income buyers. 

Additionally, according to Brown (2021), there is a strong relationship between median household income and residential battery storage adoption rates in California. The study also finds negative disparities in battery adoption rates in Zip codes with larger percentages of Black, Asian, and Hispanic residents. Defining EVs as battery electric vehicles only, the question is whether the percentage of EV registration is higher in Zip codes with higher average income. 

While previous studies have examined EV purchasing increasing in low- and middle income as well as their behavior in technology adoption, this study focuses on the associate between the average adjusted gross income (AGI) per tax return and the percentage of EV registration across California Zip codes in 2023. The study follows five sections: Introduction, Data, Methods, Results, and Discussion section. We expect there is a strong positive relationship between these variables. The results may provide some information for EV sellers when considering different sales strategies across Zip codes.


# Data {#sec-data}

```{r clean data}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| output: false


# Raw data

Vehicle_Raw_Data <- read_csv("DataP1/vehicle-fuel-type-count-by-zip-code-2023.csv")
Income_Raw_Data <- read_csv("DataP1/2024_personal_income_tax_statistics_by_zip_code.csv")


#--------------------  Vehicle Date -------------------

# rename ZipCode
Vehicle_Raw_Data <- Vehicle_Raw_Data |> rename(ZipCode = "ZIP Code")

# Clean Vehicle Date
Vehicle_Clean <- Vehicle_Raw_Data |>
                              filter(Duty == "Light") |>
                              group_by(ZipCode) |>
                              summarize(
                                Total_Light_Vehicles = sum(Vehicles, na.rm = TRUE),
                                EV = sum(Vehicles[Fuel == "Battery Electric"], na.rm = TRUE),
                                EV_Percentage = EV/Total_Light_Vehicles * 100)

# Vehicle_Clean |> count(ZipCode) |> filter(n>1)
Vehicle_Zip <- n_distinct(Vehicle_Clean$ZipCode)


# Total light vehicles registered in California
Total_Light_Vehicles <- sum(Vehicle_Clean$Total_Light_Vehicles, na.rm = TRUE)


#--------------------  Income Date -------------------

# Check if any Zip code have muliple rows
Income_Raw_Data |> filter(TaxYear == 2023) |> count(ZipCode) |> filter(n > 1)
Income_Zip <- n_distinct(Income_Raw_Data$ZipCode)

# ZIP code 93636 appears to have a duplicated row.
Income_Raw_Data |> filter(TaxYear == 2023, ZipCode == 93636)

# Clean Income Data 
Income_Clean <- Income_Raw_Data |> filter(TaxYear == 2023) |>
                    select(ZipCode, City, County, Returns, CAAGI)|>
                    distinct() |>
                    filter(!ZipCode %in% c("Suppressed", "Unallocated")) |>
                    mutate(Average_AGI = CAAGI / Returns) |>

# Income_Clean |> filter(is.na(Average_AGI) | is.infinite(Average_AGI))
# Income_Raw_Data |> filter(TaxYear == 2023, ZipCode =="90411") |> select(ZipCode, Returns, CAAGI)



# ------------------- Join Income Data and Vehicle Data based on Zip code --------------

Join_Data <- Income_Clean |> 
            inner_join(Vehicle_Clean, by = c("ZipCode" = "ZipCode")) |>
            select(ZipCode, City, County, Average_AGI, EV_Percentage)

Observations <- nrow(Join_Data)

Join_Data_without95246 <- Join_Data |> filter(ZipCode != "95246")
Observations_without95246 <- nrow(Join_Data_without95246)

# N <- n_distinct(Join_Data$ZipCode)


# Check for Data Not Matched

Income_Clean |> anti_join(Vehicle_Clean, by =  c("ZipCode" = "ZipCode"))

Vehicle_Not_Matched <- Vehicle_Clean |>
                      anti_join(Income_Clean, by = c("ZipCode" = "ZipCode"))

Vehicle_Not_Matched |> summarize(
                    Total_ZipCode = n(),
                    Total_Vehicles = sum(Total_Light_Vehicles, na.rm = TRUE),
                    Total_EV = sum(EV, na.rm = TRUE))

Vehicle_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched <- sum(Vehicle_Not_Matched$Total_Light_Vehicles, na.rm = TRUE)

Per_Vehicle_Not_Matched <- round(Vehicle_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched / sum(Vehicle_Clean$Total_Light_Vehicles, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 2)

ZipCode_Not_Matched <- nrow(Vehicle_Not_Matched)

EV_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched <- sum(Vehicle_Not_Matched$EV, na.rm = TRUE)

Per_EV_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched <- round(EV_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched / sum(Vehicle_Clean$EV, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 2)

Vehicles_Matched <- Total_Light_Vehicles - Vehicle_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched
Per_Vehicles_Matched <- round(Vehicles_Matched / Total_Light_Vehicles * 100, 2)

EV_Matched <- sum(Vehicle_Clean$EV, na.rm = TRUE) - EV_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched
Per_EV_Matched <- round(EV_Matched / sum(Vehicle_Clean$EV, na.rm = TRUE) * 100, 2)
```

The data used for this research come from two data sets extracted from the California Open Data sources. The first data set is "Personal Income Tax Statistics by Zip Code, City, and County," contains the number of tax returns, California AGI, and total tax liability for each Zip code, county, and city from tax year 1992 to 2023. The data set is collected and published by California Franchise Tax Board. It contains a total of `r format(Income_Zip, big.mark = ",")` unique Zip codes, based on the Zip codes reported on the address line of the tax returns as described by California Franchise Tax Board. These observations also include PO Box Zip codes, unique business Zip codes, and military Zip codes. Since this research focuses on average AGI per tax return for each Zip code in 2023, average AGI is calculated by dividing the total California AGI by the number of tax returns for that Zip code in tax year 2023. 

The second data set is "Vehicle Fuel Type Count by Zip Code", provides vehicle registration data of January 2024, representing the vehicle population at the end of 2023. It includes information on registered vehicles by Zip code, model year, fuel type, make, and vehicle duty classification. The data set is provided by the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), Information Policy and Liaison Branch. Zip code in the data set is defined as Zip code of vehicle registration while the vehicles count represents the number of vehicles located within Zip code jurisdiction. However, the documentation does not explicitly specify whether these Zip codes represent the vehicle owners residential addresses, mailing addresses, or the location where the vehicle primarily operated. The data set also includes Zip codes outside California, such as those in Hawaii, Nevada, and Oregon. For this research, EVs are defined as light-duty battery electric vehicles. The data are filtered to include light-duty vehicles and then aggregated by Zip code, resulting `r format(Total_Light_Vehicles, big.mark = ",")` registered vehicles across `r format(Vehicle_Zip, big.mark = ",")` unique Zip codes. The percentage of EV registrations is then calculated by dividing the number of light-duty EVs by the total number of light-duty vehicles within each Zip code.

The number of Zip codes in the light-duty registered vehicles data set is `r format(Vehicle_Zip, big.mark = ",")` which is more than `r format(Income_Zip, big.mark = ",")` Zip codes in the Personal Income Tax data set. After matching the two data sets by Zip code,  `r format(ZipCode_Not_Matched, big.mark = ",")` Zip codes from the vehicle registration data set had no corresponding tax records. These unmatched Zip codes accounted for `r format(Vehicle_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched, big.mark = ",")` light-duty vehicles (`r format(Per_Vehicle_Not_Matched, nsmall = 2)`% of all light-duty vehicles) and `r format(EV_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched, big.mark = ",")` battery electric vehicles (`r format(Per_EV_of_Vehicle_Not_Matched, nsmall = 2)`% of all battery electric vehicles). These unmatched Zip codes were excluded because this research focuses on Zip codes for which both  income tax information and vehicle registration data are available. 

The excluded observations have a relatively low EV registration rate (12,771 / 608,219 = 2.1%). Excluding these observations slightly increases the overall EV registration percentage in the remaining data set. This exclusion can effect the research results because the analysis is limited to Zip codes with available data in both data sets. However, because the unmatched Zip codes lack corresponding income data, they cannot be used to investigate whether Zip codes with higher average incomes have higher EV registration percentages. Therefore, excluding these unmatched Zip codes is necessary for this research. 

The final joined data set for this research is created by joining the income and vehicle data sets by Zip codes in which `r format( Observations, big.mark = ",")` matched Zip codes, accounting for `r format(Vehicles_Matched, big.mark = ",")` (`r format(Per_Vehicles_Matched, nsmall = 2)`% of all light-duty vehicles) and `r format(EV_Matched, big.mark = ",")` (`r format(Per_EV_Matched, big.mark = ",")` % of all battery electric vehicles). Each observation represents one matched Zip code, City, County, and includes average AGI per tax return and the percentage of EV registrations in 2023. Summary statistics for the final joined data set are presented in the @tbl-descriptive.


The association between average AGI per tax return and the percentage of EV registrations in 2023 is shown in @fig-ev-scatter.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

The simple linear regression model is used to examine the association between average AGI per tax return and the percentage of EV registrations across California Zip codes. 

$$Y_i = \beta_0 +\beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i$$

The regression coefficients are estimated using the ordinary least squares (OLS) method, which minimizes the sum of squared residuals, defined as
$$ Q(b_0,b_1) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}(Y_i-b_0-b_1X_i)^2 $$












The OLS estimates are the values of $b_0$ and $b_1$ are the values that minimize $Q$.
In this model, $Y_i$ represents the percentage of EV registrations in Zip code $i$, and $X_i$ represents the average AGI per tax return in dollars. The slope $\beta_1$ represents the expected change in EV registration percentage, measured in percentage points, for each one dollar increases in average AGI. For each \$10,000 increase in average AGI, the expected change is $10{,}000\beta_1$ percentage points. The intercept $\beta_0$ represents the expected percentage of EV registrations when the average AGI per tax return is zero. The error term $\varepsilon_i$ represents the random variation in the percentage of EV registrations that is not explained by average AGI.

R programming language version 4.4.2 is used to fit the linear regression model.

To determine whether there is sufficient evidence of a positive linear association between average AGI and the percentage of EV registrations, one-sided t-test is conducted for the slope parameter $\beta_1$ at a significance level of $\alpha$ = 0.05. The null hypothesis specifies that the population slope is zero, while the alternative hypothesis represents a positive linear association. 
$$H_0: \beta_1 = 0$$
$$H_1: \beta_1 > 0$$
The simple linear regression model assumes a linear relationship between average AGI and the expected EV registration percentage, independent errors, constant error variance, and normally distributed errors for statistical inference. Under these assumptions, the Gauss-Markov theorem states that the OLS estimators are the best linear unbiased estimators. Additionally, normally distributed errors are assumed to support statistical inference.


```{r t-test}
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| output: false

Model_summary <- summary(EV_Model_without95246)
t_value <- Model_summary$coefficients["Average_AGI", "t value"]
df <- df.residual(EV_Model_without95246)

p_value <- pt(t_value, df = df, lower.tail = FALSE)

t_value
df
p_value

```

# Results {#sec-results}

The model is $\hat{Y}_i = 1.299 + 0.00001378X_i$. The estimated intercept $b_0$ is 1.299, meaning that when the average AGI per tax return is zero, the model predicts an EV registration percentage of approximately 1.299%. However, an average AGI of zero is not typical California Zip code, so the intercept has limited practical meaning. The estimated slope $b_1$ is 0.00001378. This coefficient appears very small because average AGI is measured in dollars, so a one unit increase represents only $\$1$. That means on each $10,000 increase in average AGI per tax return is associated with an estimated increase of 0.1378 percentage points in EV registration percentage.

The one-sided t-test is conducted to determine whether average AGI is positively associated with the percentage of EV registrations. The t-value for this test is `r round(t_value, 2)`, with `r df` degrees of freedom, and the p-value is `r format.pval(p_value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)`. Since the p-value is too small, which is less than $\alpha = 0.05$, the null hypothesis $H_0$ is rejected. This provides sufficient statistical evidence of a positive linear association between average AGI and the percentage of EV registrations. However, the hypothesis test does not indicate how well the linear model explains the variations in EV registration percentages; instead, $R^2$ is used for this purpose.

The $R^2$ value for the fitted model is `r round(R_squared_without95246, 4)` indicating approximately `r round(R_squared_without95246 *100, 2)`% of the variation in EV registration percentages across the Zip codes is explained by average AGI. To assess the regression assumptions and evaluate the adequacy of the model, the residual versus fitted values plot and the Normal Q-Q plot are examined in @fig-residual and @fig-qq-plot, respectively. In @fig-residual, most observations are concentrated at relatively low fitted values, with residuals clustered around zero. As the fitted values increase, the residuals become more spread out, particularly in the negative direction. This pattern suggests possible heteroscedasticity, indicating that the constant error variance assumption may not hold. One observation stands apart from the others, with a negative fitted value and a large positive residual. In @fig-qq-plot, the residuals in the middle portion of the Normal Q-Q plot are relatively close to the reference line. However, the points deviate substantially from the reference line in both tails. The points in the left tail fall considerably below the reference line, while those in the right tail curve upward above it. These deviations suggest that the residuals are not fully normally distributed, particularly in the tails.

Overall, @fig-residual shows increasing residual spread as the fitted values increase, while @fig-qq-plot shows substantial deviations from the reference line in both tails. Therefore, we further examine the extreme residuals by identifying the 10 Zip codes with the largest positive residuals (@tbl-high-residual) and the 10 Zip codes with the largest negative residuals (@tbl-low-residual).

Although the observed EV registration percentages range from 0% to 26%, the response variable range from 0% to 100% in theory. So, the linear regression can predict values outside the valid range. Moreover, the bounded response variable and differences in vehicle counts across Zip codes can contribute to non-constant error variance. This is also consistent with the pattern observed in the residual plot. 

Among the ZIP codes in the top 1% of average AGI per tax return, nine appear among the 10 largest negative residuals, with average AGI ranging from  $\$619,660$ to $\$1,657,737$. Only one ZIP code in the top 1% of average AGI, ZIP code 90410, appears among the 10 largest positive residuals which the residual of 15.01 percentage points. For the 10 ZIP codes with the largest positive residuals, the observed EV registration percentages are higher than the values predicted by the linear model. Conversely, the ZIP codes with the largest negative residuals have observed EV registration percentages substantially lower than the predicted values.

The analysis shows a statistically significant positive linear association between average AGI per tax return and EV registration percentage across California Zip codes. This suggests that Zip codes with higher average income tend to have higher EV registration percentages. However, only `r round(R_squared_without95246 *100, 2)`% of the variation in EV registration percentages is explained by average AGI, indicating that other factor may also influence EV adoption. Additionally, the residual analysis shows that several Zip codes with very high average AGI have lower EV registration percentages than predicted by the model. The residual plot also suggest possible violations of the constant variance and normality assumptions, which affect the reliability of statistical inference.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The residual plot and the normal Q-Q plot suggest some concerns regarding the assumptions of the simple linear regression model. In the residual plot, since the spread of residuals increases as the fitted values increase, it indicates that the variability of EV registration percentages may change with the fitted values. On the other hand, in the normal Q-Q plot, the residuals do not closely follow the reference line and display a curved pattern, with the deviations tend to much larger in the tails. This suggests that the residual distribution differs from a normal distribution, particularly at its extremes. Regarding linearity, the residual plot exhibits systematic patterns rather than random scatter. However, the plot highlights the changing spread of the residuals more apparently than a clear nonlinear pattern. Therefore, the constant error variance and normality assumptions are not satisfied. As a result, the standard errors and p-value from the OLS regression are not reliable, although the estimated positive relationship average AGI and EV registration percentage remain. 

Some of these patterns may be related to Zip codes with extreme average AGI values. As shown in @tbl-high-residual, several Zip codes with very high average AGI have substantially lower EV registration percentages than predicted by the linear model. For example, Zip codes 94119 in San Francisco has an average AGI of approximately $\$1.66$ million, with an observed EV registration percentage of 3.54% which is lower than the predicted value of 24.14%. This results in a large negative residual of approximately 20.61 percentage points. In contrast, @tbl-low-residual shows that some Zip codes have EV registration percentages substantially higher than predicted. These differences suggest that average AGI alone does not adequately explain EV registration percentages for certain Zip codes. 

Moreover, among the Zip codes with the highest average AGI, some are PO Boxes or are located in financial hubs such as San Francisco and Los Angeles. These Zip codes do not represent typical residential areas, and Zip codes reported on tax returns may not correspond to the actual residential locations or vehicle registration locations of taxpayers. This explain why some Zip codes with extremely high average AGI have EV registration percentages lower than predicted by the linear model. However, these observations should not automatically be considered data errors and were retained in the analysis. This is because many of the Zip codes with the extreme AGI values are located in the Bay Area and Los Angeles, where very high salaries, capital gains, business profits or losses can produce unusual AGI values. Hence, these observations were retain in the analysis rather than excluded solely because of their extreme AGI values.

One limitation of this analysis is the use of average AGI as a proxy for income. This is because AGI includes income sources other than W-2 wages, such as capital gains and business profits or losses. As a result, average AGI may not accurately reflect the income of a typical person or household within a Zip code. A small number of tax returns with extremely high income or large losses can substantially affect the average AGI of a Zip code. Therefore, average AGI may not accurately represent the typical income level of residents in that area. 

Another limitation of this model is that the number of registered vehicles varies across ZIP codes, partly due to differences in population size and vehicle ownership. However, the simple linear regression model assigns equal weight to each ZIP code, regardless of the number of registered light-duty vehicles. As a result, ZIP codes with relatively few registered vehicles are treated equally to ZIP codes with much larger vehicle counts, even though their EV registration percentages may have different levels of variability. A weighted regression model could be considered in future analyses to account for these differences.

Consequently, although the hypothesis test provides strong statistical evidence of a positive linear association between average AGI and EV registration percentage, average AGI alone explains only `r round(R_squared_without95246 *100, 2)`% of the variation across ZIP codes. This indicates that a substantial portion of the variation remains unexplained by the model. Other factors may also be associated with EV registrations, such as housing type, availability of charging stations, gasoline and electricity costs, and population density. Collecting additional data on these factors and considering median income instead of average AGI may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship. Furthermore, a multiple linear regression model could be considered to examine these associations simultaneously.
